children.author: carefree-bob
children.text:
shareholder value of a company = equity = assets - liabilities.

Requiring equity > liabilities means assets > 2* liabilities.

That is nice, but not at all required for financial health. Especially for infrastructure heavy companies where the debt is used primarily to fund infrastructure buildout.

> But I want them to be valued far more realistically.

They are. That's the problem. The obligations that these companies are, on paper, supposed to meet require these valuations.

If you value Anthropic at $500b that's still a fuckload and vastly less than their obligations and a lot of people are going to say "well wait a minute how am I going to get paid".

The amount of spend going on, and planned, is insane and underpins a lot of this, and is why people are skeptical of the valuations. It has nothing to do with "Wanting" AI to fail and just a reasonable bet based on the math. For them to pay back what they have on their balance sheet entire continents will functionally be a spec in comparison, and that's really really fucking unlikely to happen.

Doubly so when you consider that there's a question of if they can be profitable to projected needed levels without fundamentally breaking some economics parts, and that this looks a lot like the overbuild of the internet during the dotcom bubble, which was also hideously overvalued at the time, for the time frame they were looking at, despite being THE literal world changing tech.

I’m not sure it’s a binary thing that contradicts.

I want AI and these companies to succeed. And I especially want new companies to succeed. But I want them to be valued far more realistically. Because if they have to be worth trillions, then there’s a real motivation to do what it takes to realize that valuation. And that’s how you birth a Zuckerberg.

I’m not rooting for them to fail. I’m rooting for the correction to happen sooner than later.

children.author: Karrot_Kream
children.text:
Ultimately the question is whether there's a pareto optimal point for intelligence models. There's 2 potential worlds:

1. Frontier models are so good that the token cost of an average task becomes miniscule, so users are incentivized to use frontier models because their sheer intelligence makes them cheaper to use.

2. There is a pareto optimal point where even if you spend more on tokens overall profits decrease because token costs rise faster than revenue does.

The "no lab has a clear lead" world leads to 2.

Yet it can do all these things when prompted.

There seems to be another magic ingredient for improving agents beyond model size & efficiency, and so far only OpenAI, Anthropic, and maybe Google know what it is.

> they are still clearly in the lead on coding and will continue to do well until someone definitively passes them.

I think the first implying the second might be a bit of a stretch. At some point, companies are going to start looking at their AI spending and start negotiating deals. OpenAI is right behind them and Anthropic is around 8x more expensive (Sol 6.1 vs Opus 5.5 based on Artificial Intelligence's cost per task; cost per token is a somewhat useless metric when different models use vastly different numbers of tokens for the same thing). Chinese models like Deepseek 4.1 Flash are cheap, can be self-hosted, and while certainly behind Claude Opus 5.5, are still good.

Lots of companies buy "inferior" products like Microsoft Teams. Over the next 5 years, it seems likely that many models will get really good to the point that people often won't be able to tell any difference. Even if something isn't "definitively" better, companies might say "our engineers can't tell the difference and we're cutting our costs by 85%."

It's not absurd to think that a company would use its own harness or an open source harness and/or put a proxy in to route requests variably. For two months, they have engineers using different models unbeknownst to them and they measure things like how often the engineers have to correct or redirect the model. At the end of two months, they might find little difference in performance and switch to a much lower cost model.

It's not like it'd be crazy hard to analyze workers frustration as they did their jobs and figure out if one model was actually better. They could log all the conversations and it's not like AI can't easily determine things like "no, that's completely wrong" as a phrase showing that the agent was really off base.

I think a big part of the next 5-10 years is going to be about cost/efficiency.

children.author: calebkaiser
children.text:
I think this dynamic is underappreciated. Another thing I see in working with different companies (consulting) and discussing with colleagues at different jobs is that we as humans tend to do a pretty bad job of modeling business outcomes and the dynamics that govern them. There are lots of outcomes where you can identify one contributing role, increase the productivity for that role by a significant factor, and still ultimately not move the needle much, because the constraints span multiple functions.

As an example outside of software engineering, a lot of people in marketing roles have found agents to be incredibly useful for particular tasks. I've talked to multiple people who wouldn't standardly be classified as "technical hires" who are using Claude to manage things like digital advertising. It's valuable here because managing campaigns on a platform like Google or LinkedIn involves a ton of granular tweaking and analysis. Every performance marketer makes tradeoffs around what they're realistically able to spend time doing, and what makes the biggest impact. So if you have 250 campaigns that you manage solo, you likely don't have the time to really manually optimize the bidding and budget for each campaign every couple of days based on new data. You can only try so many new angles, because creating new media is time consuming. You don't have time to construct custom experiences on-page for every particular campaign. There's a whole industry of tools that turn a tidy profit automating parts of this for this reason. And agents are really good at it, because a lot of it is just applying the same analysis over and over again.

But for a lot of startups, increasing traffic from ads 20% while decreasing spend is a good outcome, but it doesn't actually turn into revenue. The product itself might just be limited, and already being discovered by the narrow segment of potential users who find it valuable enough to pay. Or the sales process might be kind of busted, meaning the team will really only close a certain volume of new deals in a given month, no matter how much inbound they have. Or some combination of all of the above.

If it's just one marketer using an agent to optimize their advertising, there's not a lot they can do about the other constraints. And so what you end up with is one employee who feels really productive and sings the praises of Claude, but not a meaningful lift in the higher level outcomes you care about, and the analysis gets messy. In an ideal world, everyone realizes where the other bottlenecks are, but that's a genuinely hard thing to do and people have complicating incentives.

I don't think this is a particularly new problem. It feels identical to any other situation where a department asks for a tool, loves it, and it doesn't really make a difference to the bottom line or make anyone else's life easier in noticeable ways.

Anthropic S1 had numbers up till Q2. Many people speculated that Q3 numbers were lower because many companies had moved away from "token as measure of productivity" or tokenmaxxing. Anthropic Q3 numbers proved that theory.

As the article notes the growth is still huge. But it has slowed down relative to what they were growing.

This piece was published in mid-October based on rumored numbers.

Anthropic released their Q3 numbers today which show:

- $16.96B in revenue Q3

- Up 47% quarter over quarter (Q2 was $11.6B)

- Up >1000% year over year

I wouldn't say their growth "flattened"? Their price drops in September dramatically increased Claude token consumption per OpenRouter

Sources: https://www.anthropic.com/news/s1-sec; https://openrouter.ai/anthropic

children.text:
I didn't think I needed to spell it out for the HN crowd, since folks talk about the Chinese models every day. But, OK...

At least three Chinese companies have bragged about their latest models being trained and/or served on Chinese-made GPUs. Literally within the past 24 hours, LongCat spent a large portion of their release announcement for 2.5 bragging about how efficient their training process is and that it runs on domestic (Chinese) GPUs: "LongCat-2.5 uses long-sequence training during both mid-training and SFT. With less than 80 GB of memory per domestic AI accelerator, the training system prioritizes memory efficiency and aligns its parallelism with the supernode architecture."

https://longcat.ai/blog/longcat-2.5/

DeepSeek has repeatedly blown the curve in terms of how efficiently a model can be trained and served, Xiaomi and Z.ai aren't far behind, and have also discussed training and serving on home-grown hardware. I'm sure you can search Arxiv for all of the papers from these providers (DeepSeek, in particular, who document seemingly everything, even when they're doing something ahead of the US providers) as well as I can.

> 3. cornering the market on memory and GPUs (even if they sit in a warehouse for months or years before going online, as long as it drives up the price for competitors) only works if your competitors don't figure out how to do it more efficiently and on alternative platforms.

My understanding is that the GPU market is largely sold out for the next few years?

What exactly is the threat here? Like, which specific competitors, what efficiency improvements, what alternate platforms?

This is why Musk rushed consolidating xAI with Spacex and rushed to an IPO. And, why it was so important to him that Nasdaq and Russell rewrite their rules so he could dip into everyone's retirement accounts as quickly as possible. I don't think he's particularly bright, but he has an incredible cunning about how markets behave and how to manipulate those markets to his ends.

The writing was already on the wall about a lot of things WRT the AI market: 1. there's a limit to how much money will be thrown at it before investors expect a return, and that limit is fast approaching, 2. it's turning out "intelligence" is going to be a commodity and it's not much of a moat, 3. cornering the market on memory and GPUs (even if they sit in a warehouse for months or years before going online, as long as it drives up the price for competitors) only works if your competitors don't figure out how to do it more efficiently and on alternative platforms.

Spacex also soaked up a lot of the retail appetite for AI, even though it's an also-ran that barely qualifies, in terms of enterprise and government usage (and for good reasons, both technical and otherwise). Every other AI IPO is going to be facing a more pessimistic market, especially if we continue to be in a tough economic environment.

In short: They waited too long, now they're in a world where they've burned so much money people expect them to deliver something that no one in the AI industry probably can deliver: a monopoly-like hold on a huge percentage of the market, and to invent a bunch of new markets that aren't currently buying AI. They have to have a dominant position for this to work because they have to be able to set their price higher than is standard now, without everyone fleeing to other cheaper providers. And, when the market for memory and GPUs finally gets back to normal and supply catches up with demand, I'd wager a lot of companies, and even individuals, are going to get real serious about open models and self-hosting (unless prices remain competitive for the hosted models).
